item.title: Theory of mind, autism-like traits, executive functions, and structural brain MRI findings in children with neurofibromatosis type 1.
item.description:
European journal of pediatrics
This study aimed to examine social-cognitive difficulties in children with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) by jointly investigating theory of mind (ToM), executive functions, and autism-like traits and to explore whether children with NF1 show structural differences in brain regions commonly implicated in social cognition and executive functioning. In this two-center cross-sectional study, 41 children aged 8-18 years were included, comprising 21 children with NF1 and 20 age- and sex-matched typically developing children. Participants underwent behavioral assessment, including parent-reported autism-like traits, everyday executive functioning, and direct measures of ToM. Structural brain MRI data were analyzed using automated volumetric and cortical thickness measures, focusing on these regions. Children with NF1 showed higher autism-like traits, lower everyday executive functioning in play and social routines, and poorer performance on an advanced ToM task. The NF1 group also had larger global brain volume reflecting widespread white matter expansion; lower cortical gray matter proportion and thickness in frontal, temporal, parietal, cingulate, and limbic regions; and larger subcortical structures including the amygdala, hippocampus, and thalamus. Exploratory within-group brain-behavior correlations were few and selective, none survived multiple-comparison correction, and none involved autism-like traits. Conclusion Children with NF1 display a multidimensional profile of social-cognitive difficulties together with structural differences indicating an imbalance between cortical and subcortical regions typically involved in social cognition. These structural differences offer a possible neurobiological substrate for the social-cognitive difficulties observed in NF1. Whether they account for these difficulties remains to be tested in samples powered to examine brain-behavior associations directly. What is known • Children with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) frequently show executive dysfunction, autism-like traits, and theory of mind (ToM) difficulties. • These domains have rarely been examined jointly, or alongside brain structure, in the same children. What is new • Autism-like traits, everyday executive difficulties, and poorer ToM co-occurred in children with NF1. • The same children showed reduced cortical thickness and proportion with enlarged subcortical structures in regions implicated in social cognition, a candidate substrate for future brain-behavior studies.

item.title: Functional and structural neuroplasticity of motor system in hemiplegic cerebral palsy
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Hemiplegic cerebral palsy results from a unilateral prenatal or perinatal brain injury and causes motor impairments in the contralateral side of the body. Variable functional outcomes among children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy despite similar lesion extent suggest that developmental neuroplasticity and brain reorganization contribute to motor function. By using multimodal neuroimaging, we characterize the structural and functional reorganization of the motor system and examine its associations with lesion characteristics and upper-limb performance. We examined 26 children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy and 26 typically developing controls using electromagnetic source imaging to map the primary motor cortex and characterize movement-related oscillations across physiologically relevant frequency bands, navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation to assess motor cortical excitability and lateralization, and functionally guided diffusion-weighted MRI to evaluate the structural integrity of descending motor and motor commissural fibers. We further assessed upper-limb function using Melbourne Assessment 2 and examined multimodal relationships using correlation, cross-validated latent-variable, and mediation analyses. Children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy showed microstructural abnormalities in the descending motor and motor commissural fibers, characterized by lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean, axial, and radial diffusivity (all P < 0.05). The navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation identified ipsilateral corticospinal projections from the less affected hemisphere in 17 of 22 children (77%) with hemiplegic cerebral palsy, accompanied by reduced contralesional primary motor cortex lateralization ( P < 0.05). The hemiplegic cerebral palsy group also exhibited hemisphere-specific abnormalities in movement-related oscillations, including reduced theta synchronization in the contralesional hemisphere and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization in the ipsilesional hemisphere (all P < 0.05). Larger lesions were associated with poorer motor performance ( Rho = −0.74 to −0.57, P < 0.05). Reduced descending motor fiber integrity was associated with impaired dexterity and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization ( Rho = −0.51 to 0.62, P < 0.05), while motor commissural fiber integrity was associated with corticospinal motor lateralization ( Rho = −0.45 to 0.41, P < 0.05). A cross-validated multimodal structural-functional model predicted motor function (Q² = 0.42, P ≤ 0.001) more accurately than structural measures alone (Q² = 0.25). Beta-band desynchronization mediated the association between descending motor fiber integrity and motor performance (indirect effect = 0.12 SD, 95% CI 0.03–0.24). Developmental motor neuroplasticity in hemiplegic cerebral palsy reflects an integrated structure-physiology-behavior process rather than the direct consequence of lesion burden alone. Multimodal biomarkers may improve prognostication and support individualized rehabilitation and neuromodulation.

item.title: Diffusion-based vertex-wise connectomics encodes individual differences in cognition, affect and pathology
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
No two brains are wired alike, and much of a person’s cognitive and clinical state is written in this individual variation, not in the group average. Structural connectomes, however, are typically read through group atlases that summarize connectivity into regional averages, leaving this individual signal untapped. We build a vertex-wise structural connectome, in which every cortical surface vertex is a node, and apply it across the Alzheimer’s continuum. Using an independent dataset for methodological development and a multisite cohort of 317 participants from ADNI-4, we show that connection distance and organizational scale form a nested hierarchy, from a long-range backbone to fine, short-range structure. The individual fingerprint is strongest in medium- and short-range connections and becomes less distinctive as connectivity is pooled into atlas parcels. This individual structure can be recovered across spatial scales, although its fidelity depends on diffusion acquisition quality, with multishell data providing a more informative reference than single-shell data. In the aging brain, an individually referenced balance between short- and long-range connectivity is associated with episodic memory, cognitive reserve, depressive symptoms, and shared molecular pathology. While cognitive associations largely reflect diagnostic differences, associations with depressive symptoms and pathology burden remain detectable after adjustment for diagnosis. These findings show that individual structural connectomes retain clinically and biologically relevant variation that is not fully captured by diagnostic classification or group-level summaries.

item.title: Acute-Phase Superior Longitudinal Fasciculus Microstructure, Trail Making Performance and Off-Road Driving Screening After First-Ever Stroke: A Pilot Study.
item.description:
Brain sciences
Resuming driving is a priority for stroke survivors, but on-road assessment is costly and often unavailable, leaving clinicians to triage at the bedside with limited evidence. The neural basis of impaired performance on off-road driving screening after stroke is largely uncharacterised and has not been examined at the level of individual white matter pathways. We tested whether microstructural integrity of the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) differs between first-ever stroke patients who pass and those who fail an off-road driving screening assessment, independently of age, sex and education, and whether any such difference is accompanied by impairment in attention. Twenty-two patients with first-ever ischaemic stroke underwent diffusion tensor imaging a median of four days after onset (range 2-20), followed by a standardised off-road driving screening assessment and cognitive assessment before discharge conducted by different clinicians under reciprocal blinding. The affected-hemisphere SLF was specified in advance as the tract of interest. The primary outcome was within-subject normalised fractional anisotropy (FA), i.e., the tract value minus that patient's mean across all reconstructed tracts, which removes a diffusivity shift affecting all reconstructed tracts equally. This normalisation does not remove regionally heterogeneous change, and the FA asymmetry index is additionally reported as a sensitivity analysis. Differences in continuous measures are reported as Hedges' g with 95% confidence intervals and categorical comparisons as exact p values. Ten of 22 patients (45%) failed. The normalised SLF FA of the affected hemisphere was lower in these patients (g = -0.93, 95% CI -1.82 to -0.05), and the estimate remained above one standard deviation across a nested covariate sequence (d = -0.97 to -1.50), although significance was not retained once global cognition, a plausible intermediate, was included (Model 3, p = 0.060). The group difference did not reach significance on the fractional anisotropy asymmetry index (g = -0.55, 95% CI -1.41 to 0.30, p = 0.176), and the group-by-hemisphere interaction was not significant (p = 0.186). Neither lesion volume nor lesion side predicted outcome. Seven of the ten failing patients could not complete the Trail Making Test, Part B, versus none of the twelve passing patients (p < 0.001). Lesion involvement of an atlas-defined SLF did not differ between groups; among the 12 patients whose lesion spared that tract the group difference was larger than in the cohort as a whole (g = -1.43, p = 0.018). Correlations between SLF anisotropy and cognitive performance did not survive normalisation together with removal of censored observations. No comparison in the wider exploratory panel of WM tracts survived correction for multiple comparisons. Failure on off-road driving screening was associated with lower anisotropy in a fronto-parieto-temporal association pathway (i.e., the SLF) and with inability to complete a timed attentional task, beyond what conventional lesion descriptors explained. The imaging difference was not robust across alternative specifications, and reduced anisotropy at this timepoint is compatible with several processes rather than demonstrating structural disconnection. The attentional differences were largely accounted for by education, from which they could not be separated at this sample size. These preliminary findings require replication.

item.title: Genetic, metabolic and hippocampal myelin contributions to episodic memory ageing
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract There is ongoing controversy about the role of the apolipoprotein-E (APOE) genotype in modulating cognitive trajectories in healthy ageing and Alzheimer’s disease. We investigated associations between APOE genotype, cardiometabolic and inflammatory profiles, lifestyle, and hippocampal microstructure with late-life episodic memory trajectories in a community-dwelling, mid-to-old-age cohort. The genotyped sample (n = 5325) with follow-up spanning over 20 years included nested cognitive (n = 1378) and neuroimaging subsamples (n = 301). We first tested whether the APOE ε4 allele was associated with systemic physiological profiles across adulthood, followed by assessment of APOE associations with cognitive ageing trajectories and their relationships with health profiles and MRI markers of hippocampal myelination. APOE ε4 carrier status was associated with an adverse lipid-related metabolic profile across adulthood. In late-life, APOE ε4 was selectively associated with steeper age-related episodic memory decline across cognitive domains examined, with effects emerging in the eighth decade of life and evident already among heterozygous carriers. Individual metabolic, inflammatory, cardiovascular, and lifestyle markers did not account for this APOE ε4-related memory effect. When considered jointly within their respective domains, adverse metabolic burden was associated with poorer episodic memory performance and reduced odds of memory maintenance, whereas a favorable lifestyle profile was associated with better episodic memory function, independently of APOE genotype. The association between hippocampal myelin content and steepness of episodic memory trajectories was stronger in APOE ε4 carriers, while hippocampal volume showed only a trend. These findings indicate that APOE ε4 is primarily linked to episodic memory decline dynamics, with hippocampal myelin marking trajectory differences, whereas peripheral metabolic burden and lifestyle relates to memory performance level.
